findings.summary: Custom type parser ignores the `format` argument when overriding, so binary-format DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ would return a Buffer instead of a string
findings.evidence: `datasourceTypeParser = (oid, format) => RAW_TEXT_OIDS.has(oid) ? (value: string) => value : getDefaultParser(oid, format)` — the identity branch is returned regardless of `format`. pg calls getTypeParser(oid, 'binary') for binary result fields, where the parser receives a Buffer; returning it unchanged yields a Buffer that `toCell` will render as `{"type":"Buffer",...}` instead of a date string. The override should only apply when format === 'text'.

findings.summary: Array date/time OIDs (_date 1182, _timestamp 1115, _timestamptz 1185) are not in RAW_TEXT_OIDS, so array columns still get timezone-shifted JS Dates
findings.evidence: RAW_TEXT_OIDS contains only the scalar DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ OIDs. pg-types' array parsers for `date[]`, `timestamp[]`, `timestamptz[]` are registered under separate OIDs and parse elements with their own internal date parser, not via our getTypeParser override — so the exact timezone-shift bug the comment says it fixes still occurs for array-typed columns, producing inconsistent formatting (Date objects → JSON.stringify inside toCell) versus scalar columns.

findings.summary: `SET DateStyle = 'ISO, MDY'` changes interpretation of ambiguous date literals inside user queries
findings.evidence: DateStyle's second component controls *input* parsing order. Forcing MDY means a user query containing e.g. `WHERE d = '01/02/2025'` is now interpreted as Jan 2 even on servers whose default is DMY, silently changing query results. Only the output style ('ISO') is needed for the stated goal; the input order should be left at the server default (`SET DateStyle = 'ISO'` keeps the existing order).

findings.summary: `types.getTypeParser` is captured unbound; if pg-types ever dispatches on `this`, the fallback call throws at query time
findings.evidence: `const getDefaultParser = types.getTypeParser as (...)` detaches the method from the `types` module object. It works today because pg-types' module-level getTypeParser is a plain function, but any pg upgrade that turns it into a method using `this` (as TypeOverrides.getTypeParser already does) makes every non-date column parse throw a TypeError inside executeQuery.

findings.summary: toCell's object branch changes rendering of Buffer/array values and can throw on non-serializable values
findings.evidence: `JSON.stringify(val)` for `typeof val === 'object'` turns a bytea Buffer into `{"type":"Buffer","data":[...]}` and a `text[]` into `["a","b"]` (previously `String(val)` gave the text / `a,b`). JSON.stringify also throws TypeError on circular structures or BigInt-containing objects, which would propagate out of `loadQueryResults` and break rendering of the whole result set; there is no try/catch fallback to String(val).

findings.summary: Cleanup query inside `finally` can mask the original failure
findings.evidence: `finally { await rawClient.query(`DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ${table}`); await rawClient.end(); }` — if the loop failed because the raw connection died, the DROP rejects and replaces the real assertion error, and `rawClient.end()` is then never called (connection leak). The other tests in this file wrap cleanup so the connection is always ended.

findings.summary: Adding the two new SET statements silently broke the 'converts query runtime failures to bad request' test — it now throws on `SET TimeZone`, not on the query under test
findings.evidence: The mock at datasource.service.spec.ts:153-159 only special-cases `sql.startsWith('SET statement_timeout')` and throws for everything else. After the diff, `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` (service.ts:145) is now the second statement issued, so the mock throws there. The test still passes (BadRequestException is raised) but it no longer exercises the intended path — a real query failure on the wrapped SELECT. The wrapped query is never even reached, so this test can no longer fail if error mapping around the actual query breaks. The mock's session-setup branch should be widened to any `SET ` prefix.

findings.summary: Existing exact assertions were loosened to String()-coerced comparisons, which pass regardless of the value's runtime type — precisely the thing this change affects

findings.summary: SQL statement injection: validateSelectQuery validates a comment-stripped copy of the query, but executeQuery interpolates the ORIGINAL string into a simple-protocol query, so DDL/DML can be smuggled past the read-only guard
findings.evidence:
sql-validator.ts:28-31 builds `withoutComments` by regex-stripping `--...` to end-of-line and `/*...*/`, and every subsequent check (first-token, FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS at :47-57, multi-statement split at :60-61) runs on that stripped copy. datasource.service.ts:148 then executes the untouched `dto.query`: `SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001`, and pg's `client.query(string)` uses the simple query protocol, which executes multiple `;`-separated statements.

The regex does not understand string literals or quoted identifiers, so a `--` inside a quoted identifier truncates validation while remaining ordinary SQL to Postgres. Attacker (any authenticated workspace member who passes the controller's assertMember check at datasource.controller.ts:140) POSTs to /datasources/:id/query with:

  SELECT 1 AS "x--" ) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1

Validator view after comment stripping: `SELECT 1 AS "x` → first token SELECT (ok), no forbidden keyword (DROP was eaten by the `--` rule), no `;` (also eaten) → {valid: true}.
Actually executed at line 148: `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS "x--" ) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three complete statements, the middle one destructive. The same trick smuggles UPDATE/DELETE/COPY/GRANT. Pre-existing code, but it is the guard on the line this diff edits and nothing in the change (or in sql-validator.spec.ts, which only tests the naive `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE users` case) closes it. Fix: validate and execute the exact same string, or better, reject on a real SQL parse / use a read-only role + read-only transaction.

findings.summary: TLS certificate verification permanently disabled for datasource connections (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), so "SSL enabled" gives no MITM protection for credentials or query data
findings.evidence: createClient — the object literal this diff modifies (adds `types` at line 204) — passes `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. With verification off, any network attacker between the app and the remote Postgres can present a self-signed cert, terminate the TLS session, and read/modify the decrypted datasource password (decrypt(ds.password) at line 201) and all query results. This is the only rejectUnauthorized in packages/* (grep), so there is no CA-pinning path elsewhere. Users who tick sslEnabled reasonably believe the channel is authenticated; it is only encrypted.

findings.summary: SSRF / internal port scanning: user-supplied host+port are connected to with no allowlist, and raw driver errors are returned to the caller, making the backend an oracle for the internal network
findings.evidence: CreateDataSourceDto (datasource.dto.ts:17-25) only length/range-checks host and port — no denylist for 127.0.0.1, ::1, 169.254.169.254, or RFC1918 ranges. createClient (datasource.service.ts:196-205) connects wherever the user points it. testConnection returns `{ success:false, error: (error as Error).message }` (line 121) and executeQuery rethrows the raw pg error message (line 168-170). An authenticated user can therefore distinguish 'ECONNREFUSED' vs. connect-timeout vs. protocol errors per host:port and map internal services, and can reach services the app can reach but they cannot. The 10s connectionTimeoutMillis bounds but does not prevent scanning.

findings.summary: Raw Postgres error text is forwarded verbatim to API clients, leaking schema/internal detail
findings.evidence: executeQuery catch block throws `new BadRequestException(pgError.message)` with the driver's message unchanged. Postgres messages include table/column names, function bodies in some cases, and host/socket paths for connection errors, giving an attacker free schema enumeration on top of the injection vector above. Prefer a generic message plus server-side logging (and make sure nothing logs decrypt(ds.password)).

The service (datasource.service.ts:143-145) now issues `SET TimeZone = 'UTC'` as the second statement, so the mock throws there and the wrapped SELECT at datasource.service.ts:148-150 is never executed. The query 'SELECT * FROM FROM' does pass validateSelectQuery (sql-validator.ts:38-57), so execution genuinely reaches the client and fails at session setup. finding.summary: No unit test covers the new `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` client option or the raw-text parser itself
finding.evidence: The behavioral core of the diff is `datasourceTypeParser` returning identity for DATE/TIMESTAMP/TIMESTAMPTZ and delegating otherwise (service.ts:22-36), wired in at service.ts:205. In datasource.service.spec.ts the entire `createClient` method is spied out and replaced with a hand-rolled mock (lines 120-122, 161-163), so the option object is never constructed or asserted — the unit suite cannot fail if the parser wiring is dropped or the OID set is wrong. `datasourceTypeParser` is module-private and not exported, so it is untestable in isolation. The only coverage is packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts, which is gated behind `describeDb` (RUN_DB_INTEGRATION_TESTS === 'true', integration-helpers.ts:10-12) and therefore skipped in the ordinary jest run.

verdict.reason:
The claim that the raw-text parser wiring has no meaningful test that can fail is false. `packages/backend/test/database.e2e-spec.ts` ("check correct cell values for all pg built-in types", lines 199-307) drives real queries through `DataSourceService.executeQuery`, i.e. through the actual `createClient` that sets `types: { getTypeParser: datasourceTypeParser }` (datasource.service.ts:196-205) — nothing is mocked there. It asserts exact cell values for precisely the three OIDs in `RAW_TEXT_OIDS`: DATE -> '2025-06-15' (line 250), TIMESTAMP -> '2025-06-15 14:30:00' (line 252), TIMESTAMPTZ -> '2025-06-15 05:30:00+00' (line 253), plus dataTypeID checks (line 300). This assertion is not vacuous: without the parser wiring pg returns JS `Date` objects and `toCell` (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:32-36) renders them via `toISOString()` as e.g. '2025-06-15T14:30:00.000Z', so the test fails if the parser is dropped or the OID set is wrong.

The reviewer's mitigating premise — that this suite is skipped and therefore not on the gate — does not hold: `.github/workflows/ci.yml:164-176` defines the `verify-integration` job with `RUN_DB_INTEGRATION_TESTS: "true"` and a Postgres service, and step "Verify Integration Lane" (ci.yml:260-262) runs `pnpm verify:integration`, which (scripts/verify-integration.mjs:10, 46) sets the flag and runs `pnpm backend test:e2e` -> `jest --config ./test/jest-e2e.json` whose testRegex `test/.*\.e2e-spec\.ts$` (test/jest-e2e.json:5) matches database.e2e-spec.ts. `scripts/verify-ci.mjs:21` sets the same flag locally. samples.summary: SQL statement injection: validateSelectQuery validates a comment-stripped copy of the query, but executeQuery interpolates the ORIGINAL string into a simple-protocol query, so DDL/DML can be smuggled past the read-only guard
samples.evidence:
sql-validator.ts:28-31 builds `withoutComments` by regex-stripping `--...` to end-of-line and `/*...*/`, and every subsequent check (first-token, FORBIDDEN_KEYWORDS at :47-57, multi-statement split at :60-61) runs on that stripped copy. datasource.service.ts:148 then executes the untouched `dto.query`: `SELECT * FROM (${dto.query}) AS _q LIMIT 10001`, and pg's `client.query(string)` uses the simple query protocol, which executes multiple `;`-separated statements.

The regex does not understand string literals or quoted identifiers, so a `--` inside a quoted identifier truncates validation while remaining ordinary SQL to Postgres. Attacker (any authenticated workspace member who passes the controller's assertMember check at datasource.controller.ts:140) POSTs to /datasources/:id/query with:

  SELECT 1 AS "x--" ) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1

Validator view after comment stripping: `SELECT 1 AS "x` → first token SELECT (ok), no forbidden keyword (DROP was eaten by the `--` rule), no `;` (also eaten) → {valid: true}.
Actually executed at line 148: `SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS "x--" ) AS q; DROP TABLE users; SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1) AS _q LIMIT 10001` — three complete statements, the middle one destructive. The same trick smuggles UPDATE/DELETE/COPY/GRANT. Pre-existing code, but it is the guard on the line this diff edits and nothing in the change (or in sql-validator.spec.ts, which only tests the naive `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE users` case) closes it. Fix: validate and execute the exact same string, or better, reject on a real SQL parse / use a read-only role + read-only transaction.

samples.summary: TLS certificate verification permanently disabled for datasource connections (`rejectUnauthorized: false`), so "SSL enabled" gives no MITM protection for credentials or query data
samples.evidence: createClient — the object literal this diff modifies (adds `types` at line 204) — passes `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`. With verification off, any network attacker between the app and the remote Postgres can present a self-signed cert, terminate the TLS session, and read/modify the decrypted datasource password (decrypt(ds.password) at line 201) and all query results. This is the only rejectUnauthorized in packages/* (grep), so there is no CA-pinning path elsewhere. Users who tick sslEnabled reasonably believe the channel is authenticated; it is only encrypted.

samples.summary: SSRF / internal port scanning: user-supplied host+port are connected to with no allowlist, and raw driver errors are returned to the caller, making the backend an oracle for the internal network
samples.evidence: CreateDataSourceDto (datasource.dto.ts:17-25) only length/range-checks host and port — no denylist for 127.0.0.1, ::1, 169.254.169.254, or RFC1918 ranges. createClient (datasource.service.ts:196-205) connects wherever the user points it. testConnection returns `{ success:false, error: (error as Error).message }` (line 121) and executeQuery rethrows the raw pg error message (line 168-170). An authenticated user can therefore distinguish 'ECONNREFUSED' vs. connect-timeout vs. protocol errors per host:port and map internal services, and can reach services the app can reach but they cannot. The 10s connectionTimeoutMillis bounds but does not prevent scanning.

samples.summary: Raw Postgres error text is forwarded verbatim to API clients, leaking schema/internal detail
samples.evidence: executeQuery catch block throws `new BadRequestException(pgError.message)` with the driver's message unchanged. Postgres messages include table/column names, function bodies in some cases, and host/socket paths for connection errors, giving an attacker free schema enumeration on top of the injection vector above. Prefer a generic message plus server-side logging (and make sure nothing logs decrypt(ds.password)).
